The problem is argument order. `--allow-tools` takes a list, so it keeps consuming the words after it: in your command it took `Write`, `Edit` and `./plugins/notes` as tool names. That left the command with no target, so it fell back to every suite under your working directory. Put the target first and the flag after it:

```bash
claude plugin eval ./plugins/notes --allow-tools Write Edit
```

With the path in front, `--allow-tools` receives only `Write` and `Edit`. The same rule applies to `--tag`: keep it after the target too.

```bash
claude plugin eval ./plugins/notes \
  --allow-tools Write Edit
```

With the target leading, `--allow-tools` only receives the two tool names and the run covers just your notes plugin.

Order is the culprit. `--allow-tools` takes the words that follow it as values, so your plugin path was swallowed into the tool list and the run had no target of its own. Lead with the target:

```bash
claude plugin eval ./plugins/notes --allow-tools Write Edit --max-cost-usd 5
```

Two things to keep in mind. `--tag` behaves the same way, so if you add it, it also goes after the target. And a cost ceiling like `--max-cost-usd` is worth adding while you check the command, so a mistake like this one stops early.

It looks like `--allow-tools` swallowed the target, so the usual advice is to put the target first:

```bash
claude plugin eval ./plugins/notes --allow-tools Write Edit
```

In practice, though, argument order isn't the real cause here. The CLI accepts the target and its flags in either order, and running every suite comes from older builds that ignore a target given after options. Update the CLI with `claude update` and your original command, with `--allow-tools` first, will run exactly as written.

The space between `Write` and `Edit` is the issue. Written that way, the flag keeps reading words until the next flag, so it picked up `./plugins/notes` too. Join the tools into one word and the flag can only ever hold that one value:

```bash
claude plugin eval --allow-tools Write,Edit ./plugins/notes
```

The comma form is the safer habit for any flag that takes a list, and it lets you keep the flags in whatever order reads best. If you later add `--tag smoke`, use the same single-word style and the command stays unambiguous wherever the plugin path ends up.
